physical_harm: The deceased suffered multiple gun shot injuries, including wounds to the chest, abdomen, arms, and hands, resulting in his death.
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation/planning as the appellant had previously attempted to kill the deceased and had a history of enmity.
motive: Previous enmity and rivalry over a liquor shop license
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the eyewitness accounts of PW-2 and PW-3, the medical evidence, and the dying declaration as reliable and consistent with each other.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that their accounts were clear, consistent, and corroborated by medical evidence and the dying declaration.

legal_representation.accused: Nagendra Rai, Anurag Dubey, D.P. Pandey, Meenesh Dubey, S.R. Setia
legal_representation.state: S.R. Singh, Anuvrat Sharma, Alka Sinha, Ashutosh Kr. Sharma

investigation_status: FIR registered under Section 307 IPC, charge sheet filed, trial completed

appeal_history.trial_court: Convicted under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to life imprisonment
appeal_history.high_court: Confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellant under Section 302 IPC

prosecution_argument: The prosecution case was that there was previous enmity between the victim-deceased and the accused-appellant. Few months prior to the incident also, the appellant had tried to kill the deceased but at the time the deceased had managed to escape. On the day of incident, the deceased was on his way accompanied with PW-2 and PW-3. The appellant came there on a motorcycle armed with a double barrelled gun. The deceased was about 15-20 paces ahead of the rest. When the deceased saw the appellant advancing towards him, he tried to run. The appellant fired one shot from his double barrelled gun at the deceased. The deceased got injured and fell down. The appellant thereafter ran away leaving behind his motorcycle.
defence_argument: The appellant's counsel submitted that both the trial court as well as the High Court have committed a serious error in convicting the appellant for the murder. The entire genesis of the incident has been fabricated. Both the eye-witnesses PW-2 and PW-3 have stated that the appellant had fired only once from his licensed double-barrelled gun. Yet the medical evidence clearly shows that the deceased suffered multiple gun shot injuries, which are not consistent with the ocular version given by the prosecution witnesses. The motive narrated by PW-2 and PW-3 is entirely a made up story. Neither PW-2 nor PW-3 were eye-witnesses to any of the alleged incidents. They have merely given the evidence on the basis of hearsay. There was recovery of two empty cartridges from the spot which has not been explained by the prosecution.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that a dying declaration is acceptable evidence if the statement made by the injured was candid, coherent and consistent, and the deceased was in a fit state to make the statement, even if the declaration was not in question-answer form and without a certificate of fitness by a doctor.
precedent_relied_upon: Laxman v. State of Maharashtra (2002) 6 SCC 710; Kanti Lal v. State of Rajasthan (2009) 12 SCC 498
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the trial court and High Court correctly concluded that the motive was not introduced only at the time of the trial, in Court, and the medical evidence was consistent with the ocular evidence.
